paragraphs: This paper connects two visual recognition tasks through a common computational problem: finding transformations that explain an observed image. One task is recognizing a previously specified three-dimensional object and determining its pose in a real scene. The other is interpreting the three-dimensional arrangement of an articulated object, whose parts can move relative to one another.

The proposed formulation treats both tasks as inverse problems. Instead of starting with an object configuration and generating its appearance, the method searches for a composition of transformations connecting two patterns. The map-seeking method makes this search tractable by exploiting an ordering property of superposed patterns and decomposing transformation spaces according to the processes that generate the observations.

The neuroscience motivation comes from visual interactions with motor-related cortex and the possibility of shared computations across cortical regions. The contribution is a computationally unified, cortically plausible account of these recognition tasks. That plausibility supports a possible computational basis for visual-motor cooperation; it does not establish that cortical circuits actually implement the proposed method.
neurips-2005-a-cortically-plausible-inve.tldr: A map-seeking method expresses object recognition and articulated pose interpretation as tractable searches for compositions of transformations.

paragraphs: This paper gives support vector machines a probabilistic interpretation by connecting their hinge loss to a model of posterior class probabilities. Specifically, the loss can be understood as a negative log-likelihood within a semiparametric model. In this interpretation, the SVM supplies the parametric part, fitted through maximum a posteriori estimation.

That connection produces a way to translate an SVM score into probability information. The result is an interval of compatible posterior probabilities, rather than a single probability assigned to each score. This distinction matters because the proposed interpretation retains a range of probability values consistent with the score instead of forcing a unique estimate.

The authors use the framework to modify SVM optimization for unbalanced classification when different mistakes carry different losses. Probability information is therefore connected directly to the consequences of classification decisions. Experiments report improvements over state-of-the-art procedures. The contribution combines a new interpretation of the training objective, an interval-valued probability mapping, and a practical adaptation for asymmetric decision costs.
neurips-2005-a-probabilistic-interpretat.tldr: A semiparametric interpretation of SVMs yields probability intervals and a way to train classifiers for unequal error costs.

paragraphs: The paper presents an infinite mixture of Gaussian process experts for relationships that are difficult to describe with one uniform model. Each mixture component combines a multivariate Gaussian distribution over inputs with a Gaussian process model over outputs. This gives each expert both an input-space description and a model of the associated output behavior.

The central design choice is to model inputs and outputs jointly, rather than specifying only outputs conditional on inputs. The authors state that this construction handles changing covariance structure, discontinuities, multiple modes, and overlapping output signals. These capabilities allow the mixture to represent different kinds of behavior within the same overall modeling framework.

Joint modeling also broadens the questions the model can answer. It supports incomplete observations and inference about inputs associated with outputs, alongside ordinary regression. The authors further argue that it gives a stronger and more consistent Bayesian specification of the gating mechanism that assigns responsibility among experts. The contribution is thus a generative formulation that expands both representation and inference.
neurips-2005-an-alternative-infinite-mix.tldr: An infinite mixture of Gaussian process experts jointly models inputs and outputs to support flexible regression, missing data, and inverse inference.

paragraphs: The paper models action understanding as reasoning backward from observed behavior to the goals that could explain it. Its Bayesian framework starts with a probabilistic model of how an intentional agent acts. The key assumption is that agents tend to choose rational actions for achieving their goals within the constraints of their environment.

Inverting that model lets an observer infer a goal and use it to predict future behavior. The authors demonstrate this process in a simple sprite-world setting, including predictions for unfamiliar situations and changed environmental constraints. Because the model connects goals, surroundings, and actions, it can explain behavior in terms of what the agent is trying to accomplish.

The model qualitatively accounts for several kinds of inference previously observed in preverbal infants. It also fits quantitative predictions made by adults in a new experiment. These findings support the framework as an account of aspects of human action understanding, with the rational-action assumption providing the link between visible behavior and inferred intentions.
neurips-2005-bayesian-models-of-human-ac.tldr: A Bayesian model infers goals and predicts actions by assuming agents tend to act rationally under environmental constraints.

paragraphs: This paper examines how reliably statistical tests compare predictive models when performance is measured using something other than classification error. Nonparametric tests had already been proposed for such comparisons, but the authors note that significance testing for these alternative measures was less common. Their goal is an empirical comparison with more classical tests across varied conditions.

The study uses a very large dataset to approximate the full population against which test behavior can be assessed. It varies class imbalance, the models being compared, the performance measure, and evaluation sample size. This design examines whether the usefulness of a statistical test persists as several important features of the comparison change.

The main finding is conditional: with sufficiently large evaluation sets, nonparametric tests are relatively reliable across all examined conditions. Evaluation size is therefore central to interpreting the result. The study provides empirical support for using these tests with a broader range of performance measures, while keeping that support tied to adequate evaluation data and the conditions investigated.
neurips-2005-benchmarking-non-parametric.tldr: Nonparametric significance tests were relatively reliable across the studied conditions when evaluation sets were sufficiently large.

paragraphs: This paper studies regularized boosting when training observations are dependent. Rather than assuming independent and identically distributed samples, it considers stationary sequences satisfying a beta-mixing condition. The question is whether the combined classifier retains statistical convergence and consistency guarantees under this structured form of dependence.

Regularization is imposed by limiting the sum of the absolute weights assigned to the base classifiers. To analyze dependent data, the proof constructs independent blocks whose distribution is close to that of the original samples. This provides a bridge between the dependent sequence and an independent-block setting that can support a consistency argument.

The authors prove consistency for the resulting composite classifiers under their conditions. Relative to the independent-sample case, dependence appears in the result through a generalized condition governing growth of the regularization parameter. The significance is that the same basic weight-restricted boosting construction can retain consistency with dependent observations, provided the regularization schedule satisfies the adapted condition. The guarantee concerns the specified stationary mixing setting.
neurips-2005-convergence-and-consistency.tldr: Weight-regularized boosting remains consistent for stationary beta-mixing observations under an adapted regularization-growth condition.

paragraphs: The paper represents a changing social network by giving each entity a position in a hidden Euclidean space. Nearby entities are more likely to share an observed link. Positions can move over time, but large movements are unlikely, allowing relationships to drift while preserving continuity between successive network states.

A second contribution makes learning practical as the network grows. The method combines suitable similarity kernels, low-dimensional kd-trees, a dynamic version of multidimensional scaling for an initial approximate placement, and conjugate-gradient optimization for refinement. The resulting approach is subquadratic in the number of entities, with amortized update time per entity of O(log n).

Experiments on synthetic and real data with up to 11,000 entities indicate linear computational scaling and better performance than four alternative approaches. The authors also illustrate the method using twelve years of NIPS co-publication data. Together, the results show how a continuous model of changing relationships can be paired with computational techniques that make sizable dynamic networks accessible.
neurips-2005-dynamic-social-network-anal.tldr: Moving latent positions model changing social relationships, while efficient geometric computations make learning practical on large networks.

paragraphs: This paper addresses a statistical pattern observed in cortical activity: neuronal firing can occur in avalanches whose event intensities follow a power-law distribution. The modeling question is how a neural network can produce this kind of collective activity. The authors present a biologically plausible extension of a neural network, with dynamical synapses identified as the central mechanism in the title.

The stated finding is that the extended network exhibits a power-law avalanche distribution across a wide range of connectivity parameters. The breadth of that range matters because connectivity determines how activity can pass through the network. The result indicates that the reported distribution is compatible with multiple connectivity settings within the proposed model.

The contribution is a model-based explanation for a feature of neuronal avalanche activity that has experimental support. Its strength lies in connecting biologically motivated network dynamics to the observed distributional pattern. The model establishes that such behavior can arise in the proposed setting; the abstract does not claim that dynamical synapses are the unique explanation for cortical avalanches.
neurips-2005-dynamical-synapses-give-ris.tldr: A biologically plausible neural network with dynamical synapses produces power-law avalanche activity across a wide range of connectivity parameters.

paragraphs: The paper converts a multistage stochastic decision problem with continuous states into a sequence of supervised learning problems. Its aim is to make policy search accessible to existing classification methods. The starting point is an optimization problem associated with trajectory-tree and random-trajectory approaches to reinforcement learning.

The algorithm applies Gauss-Seidel optimization, breaking the multistage problem into single-stage subproblems. Each of these is then reduced exactly to weighted classification, which can be handled with off-the-shelf methods. The classification weights carry the decision problem into a supervised learning formulation, allowing established classifiers to participate in constructing a policy.

The authors show that the method reaches, in finitely many steps, a solution that cannot be improved by componentwise optimization. This is a specific stopping guarantee: further improvement of an individual component is unavailable at that solution. The practical significance is a systematic route from sequential decision making to simpler learning tasks, expanding the set of classification tools that can be applied to policy search.
neurips-2005-from-weighted-classificatio.tldr: A finite-step policy-search algorithm reduces multistage decision making to weighted classification and reaches a componentwise unimprovable solution.

paragraphs: This paper presents mixed-signal hardware for separating acoustic sources and determining their locations in real time. It uses a miniature array of four microphones, arranged within a diameter of one centimeter. The system combines a gradient-flow representation of the recorded traveling waves with independent component analysis.

The gradient-flow stage turns the microphone signals into instantaneous linear mixtures of time-differentiated source signals. That representation supplies observations that ICA can separate and localize. Both processing stages are implemented as dedicated VLSI circuits, making the signal transformation and source analysis parts of a concrete micropower hardware system.

The experiments use two speech sources played through speakers positioned 1.5 meters from the array on a conference-room table. The authors report perceptually clear separation of 12 dB and precise localization. Their analysis finds that remaining multipath components are spectrally diffuse and exclude the direct path. The result demonstrates the combined representation and hardware approach in a room-based acoustic setting, where reflected sound contributes to the recorded signals.
neurips-2005-gradient-flow-independent-c.tldr: Micropower hardware combines gradient-flow processing and ICA to separate and localize speech using a miniature four-microphone array.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to learn influence among interacting sequences of actions within a team. It represents those sequences as interacting Markov chains, placing individual behavior in a setting where other participants also matter. The goal is to model both what each player does and what the team does collectively.

The proposed model is a dynamic Bayesian network with two levels. The individual level describes each player's actions, while the group level describes actions of the team as a whole. This separation gives the model an explicit representation for collective behavior alongside its representations of individual participants. Learning influence is therefore part of a structured account of behavior unfolding over time.

The authors evaluate the model on synthetic multiplayer games and a corpus of multiparty meetings, reporting evidence of its effectiveness. These two settings bring the approach to simulated team interactions and recorded group activity. The central contribution is the two-level temporal model, which brings individual action sequences and team-level actions into a shared framework for learning interaction.
neurips-2005-learning-influence-among-in.tldr: A two-level dynamic Bayesian network learns interactions among individual action sequences while representing team behavior collectively.

paragraphs: The paper develops a method for identifying a person's activities and significant places from GPS traces. Its central idea is to detect important locations and classify them jointly while accounting for higher-level context. This connects the interpretation of individual location readings to the broader activities and places those readings represent.

The system uses relational Markov networks to express a hierarchical activity model. That model encodes relationships among GPS observations, activities, and significant locations, allowing these connected quantities to participate in the same inference process. The approach therefore treats location-based recognition as a structured problem involving several related levels of description.

Efficient computation is provided through message passing based on the fast Fourier transform, which supports summation over large numbers of network nodes. The authors report significant experimental improvements over existing techniques. The contribution combines joint contextual modeling with a computational method for handling the resulting networks, showing that GPS-based activity recognition can benefit from considering activities and meaningful places together.
neurips-2005-location-based-activity-rec.tldr: A hierarchical relational model jointly identifies activities and significant places from GPS data, with efficient FFT-based inference.

paragraphs: This paper addresses a disagreement about where cerebellar motor learning occurs and where its memory is stored. Different theories and experiments have pointed to either the cerebellar flocculus or the brainstem. The authors use a dynamical-system model to explain how memory formed in the flocculus can be transferred to the brainstem.

The same framework also accounts for savings phenomena in motor learning. Within the model, brainstem learning must follow a form of Hebbian rule that depends on Purkinje-cell activity. This ties the proposed transfer mechanism to a specific relationship between neural activity and changes in synaptic strength.

The analysis describes learning through trajectories in the space of synaptic weights. Explanations and predictions about experimental situations correspond to qualitative features of those trajectories, without requiring finely tuned parameters. This matters because the model's account depends on the structure of the learning dynamics. The contribution provides a simple way to understand memory transfer and savings within one dynamical framework.
neurips-2005-modeling-memory-transfer-an.tldr: A dynamical model explains cerebellar memory transfer and savings through synaptic learning governed by Purkinje-cell activity.

paragraphs: This paper asks how a person's prior beliefs can be recovered from behavior in a psychophysics task. The approach assumes the behavior is optimal, or nearly optimal, from a Bayesian perspective. It then reasons backward from the observed behavior to the probability distribution that could have guided it.

The method is nonparametric: the prior need not belong to a predetermined family such as Gaussian distributions. Despite that flexibility, the simplest formulation uses linear programming. More general versions use maximum likelihood or maximum a posteriori estimation, and many important cases yield convex optimization problems without nonglobal local maxima. The authors also develop ways to quantify uncertainty in the recovered beliefs.

A simulated coin-flipping example demonstrates accurate inference, including precise tracking of the subject's evolving posterior as observations accumulate. The paper also briefly connects the approach to neural population coding models. Its main contribution is a computationally manageable method for estimating flexible belief distributions, with the behavioral interpretation resting on the stated assumption of near-Bayesian optimality.
neurips-2005-nonparametric-inference-of-.tldr: Assuming near-Bayesian-optimal behavior, the method infers flexible prior beliefs and quantifies uncertainty through tractable optimization.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a mean-field approximation for stochastic dynamic games, where many agents make decisions in an evolving, uncertain setting. Its aim is to sharply reduce the computational work needed to solve these games. The approximation provides a more manageable route to analyzing interactions when the number of agents becomes large.

The authors give conditions under which their method approximates an equilibrium as the agent population grows. They also derive a performance bound for a specified finite number of agents. These are complementary contributions: one explains behavior in the large-population limit, while the other helps assess approximation quality at a particular population size.

The method is applied to an important class of problems in applied microeconomics. Numerical experiments show that it substantially expands the range of economic problems that can be studied computationally. The significance is the combination of computational savings and explicit approximation analysis, with the large-population equilibrium guarantee tied to the conditions established by the authors.
neurips-2005-oblivious-equilibrium-a-mea.tldr: A mean-field approximation makes large dynamic games more tractable, with conditional equilibrium guarantees and finite-population performance bounds.

paragraphs: This paper develops temporal-difference learning for a target policy using behavior generated by another policy. Its algorithm uses function approximation while reducing variance and requiring less information about the behavior policy than earlier methods. The central device is a recognizer, which filters actions to produce a related target policy.

Because the target is constructed through this filtering relationship, importance-sampling corrections can have low variance. The paper also considers targets that depart from the behavior policy's state distribution, including potential temporally extended options, to reduce variance further. The target's relationship to the observed behavior is therefore an active part of the algorithm's design.

For linear function approximation, the authors develop a complete algorithm and prove that its updates have the same direction as on-policy TD updates, implying asymptotic convergence. A stronger information requirement result holds for state aggregation: despite using importance sampling, the algorithm needs no knowledge of the behavior policy in that case. These guarantees connect the proposed variance reduction mechanism to a concrete learning procedure.
neurips-2005-off-policy-learning-with-op.tldr: Action recognizers enable lower-variance off-policy TD learning, with convergence results and no behavior-policy knowledge required for state aggregation.

paragraphs: The paper describes an off-road robot that learns to steer directly from camera images. Training examples pair images with steering angles supplied by a human driver. The collected driving runs span varied terrain, weather, lighting, and obstacle types, giving the supervised learning system examples from a broad set of operating conditions.

The robot is a 50-centimeter truck equipped with two forward-facing wireless color cameras. A six-layer convolutional network receives one pair of unprocessed, low-resolution left and right images and predicts a steering angle. Video processing runs on a remote computer, which sends control commands to the vehicle by radio.

The authors report strong obstacle detection and avoidance in real time at speeds of two meters per second. The key contribution is the complete connection from visual observations to driving commands through supervised learning. The demonstrated system shows that human steering examples can train a convolutional network to produce useful obstacle-avoidance behavior on a physical off-road vehicle.
neurips-2005-off-road-obstacle-avoidance.tldr: A convolutional network trained on human steering examples guides an off-road robot around obstacles directly from paired camera images.

paragraphs: This paper develops a theory of how feedback increases the computational power of dynamical systems whose memory otherwise fades. It is motivated by the abundance of feedback connections in the brain. The theory implies that many such systems gain universal analog computational capabilities with non-fading memory when feedback is introduced.

A key consequence is the ability to process changing input streams according to rules held in the system's internal states. These states take the form of high-dimensional attractors. They can preserve information while still allowing the circuit to incorporate new input, providing a mechanism for maintaining context during ongoing computation.

The authors use this account to develop models of working memory, evidence integration, and reward expectation in cortical circuits. They also show applicability to conductance-based Hodgkin-Huxley neuron circuits with substantial noise reflecting in-vivo experimental conditions. The contribution links an abstract result about feedback and memory to neural models that remain responsive to incoming information while retaining internal computational state.
neurips-2005-principles-of-real-time-com.tldr: Feedback can give many fading-memory systems persistent memory and universal analog computation, supporting models of flexible cortical processing.

paragraphs: This paper demonstrates a hardware system that builds an organized retinal map from visual input. The authors describe it as the first fully hardware implementation covering the entire process from photon transduction to retinotopic self-organization. The map is formed automatically through interactions among silicon components driven by patterned illumination.

A silicon retina converts the light patterns into correlated spike trains. These signals drive silicon growth cones, which migrate toward sources of a diffusible guidance cue released by postsynaptic spikes. Their movement wires a topographic mapping, connecting the activity generated by visual input to the physical organization of the resulting neural map.

By changing the illumination pattern, the researchers steer growth cones associated with different retinal ganglion-cell types toward either segregated or coordinated retinotopic maps. This shows that the organization produced by the hardware depends on the structure of its input. The contribution is an integrated demonstration of sensory-driven map formation, with illumination influencing how different populations organize their projections.
neurips-2005-silicon-growth-cones-map-si.tldr: A silicon retina and silicon growth cones form topographic maps automatically, with illumination patterns steering their organization.

paragraphs: This paper studies policy quality when approximate value iteration represents costs using a partitioned state space. Within each partition, the optimal cost-to-go function is approximated by a constant. The analysis focuses on policies obtained from approximations at fixed points and derives bounds on how much performance those policies can lose.

The bounds reveal a benefit from choosing projection weights equal to the invariant state distribution of the policy that results. In other words, the weighting used to construct the approximation is linked to the states occupied under that policy. With this choice, the fixed points coincide with those of TD(0), connecting the weighting analysis to a temporal-difference method.

The analysis also supplies what the authors identify as the first performance-loss bound for approximate value iteration under an average-cost objective. The contribution explains why TD(0)-associated weighting can help policy quality in the specified approximation setting. The result is grounded in fixed-point performance bounds for partition-based approximators, giving the title's comparison a precise mathematical scope.
neurips-2005-td-0-leads-to-better-polici.tldr: For partition-based value approximation, performance bounds favor policy-distribution weighting that yields the same fixed points as TD(0).

paragraphs: This paper develops game-theoretic algorithms for predicting coordinated binding by multiple DNA-binding regulators. The problem involves allocating proteins both to local DNA neighborhoods and to individual binding sites. Those allocations are subject to resource constraints, so the framework considers how available proteins can be distributed across relevant locations.

The approach explicitly represents competing and coordinated binding relationships among proteins with affinity for a site or region. This matters because the allocation problem includes relationships among regulators as well as their individual affinities. The game-theoretic formulation brings these relationships and the resource constraints into the same mathematical treatment of binding.

The paper concentrates on developing and analyzing the mathematical foundations of this approach. It also gives a brief demonstration in a phage-switch setting. Its main contribution is therefore a formal algorithmic framework for coupled protein-binding decisions. The demonstration illustrates an application of that framework, while the core work concerns how constrained allocation and interactions among multiple regulators can be represented and analyzed.
neurips-2006-game-theoretic-algorithms-f.tldr: Game-theoretic algorithms model protein allocation to DNA while accounting for resource constraints and competing or coordinated binding.

paragraphs: This paper proposes kernel MaxEnt, a data transformation based on preserving maximum entropy. Its central quantity is Rényi entropy, estimated using Parzen windows. That choice makes an entropy-based criterion the foundation for constructing the transformed representation, which can then be used as an intermediate step in another learning method.

The authors show that kernel MaxEnt uses eigenvectors, giving it a computational connection to kernel principal component analysis. Despite that similarity, the two approaches can produce strikingly different transformed datasets. The shared use of eigenvectors therefore does not make their representations interchangeable: the criterion defining the transformation matters to the result.

The paper applies the new transformation to spectral clustering by replacing an intermediate kernel PCA step with kernel MaxEnt. The authors describe a major effect on performance from this substitution. The contribution connects a new representation criterion to a concrete clustering procedure, showing how changing the transformation within an existing algorithm can substantially affect its behavior.
neurips-2006-kernel-maximum-entropy-data.tldr: Kernel MaxEnt uses an entropy-based eigenvector transformation that substantially affects spectral clustering when substituted for kernel PCA.

paragraphs: The paper introduces Locally Smooth Manifold Learning, or LSML, which learns a warping function connecting a point on a manifold to its neighbors. In the image setting, the focus is on learning how to move between nearby points in the underlying structure. The learned object is therefore a local transformation that supports traversal.

The authors identify two important capabilities: recovering manifold structure in sparsely populated regions and extending beyond the support of the supplied data. These capabilities matter because the learned warping function describes relationships that can be used where observations are limited. The method's stated scope includes both movement among nearby examples and structure outside the observed support.

The proposed applications include embedding with a natural extension to new points, tangent-distance estimation, increasing video frame rate, video compression, and motion transfer. These uses connect the local transformation model to both representation and image-sequence tasks. The central contribution is a way to learn manifold movement, with the stated recovery capabilities making that movement useful beyond densely sampled portions of the data.
neurips-2006-learning-to-traverse-image-.tldr: LSML learns local warping functions to traverse image manifolds, including sparsely sampled regions and beyond the observed data support.

paragraphs: This paper gives a general way to solve ordinal regression, where labels have an order, using binary classification. The framework first derives extended examples from the original training data. It then trains a binary classifier on those examples and converts the classifier into a rule for assigning ordered labels.

The reduction comes with a mathematical connection between the two tasks: a weighted binary classification error bounds the ranking rule's mislabeling cost. This allows established binary classification methods to support ordinal prediction. It also lets known binary-classification generalization bounds be used to derive new bounds for ordinal regression.

The framework unifies existing approaches, including perceptron ranking and support vector ordinal regression, while providing a route to new algorithms. On benchmark datasets, some of the newly designed methods show advantages in both training speed and generalization over existing algorithms. The result supports the usefulness of the reduction as both an analytical framework and a practical design method, with the empirical advantages applying to the reported algorithms and comparisons.
neurips-2006-ordinal-regression-by-exten.tldr: A reduction from ordinal regression to binary classification transfers learning methods and error bounds while yielding competitive new algorithms.

paragraphs: This paper simplifies inference for linear Gaussian state-space models whose parameters receive a Bayesian treatment. Variational Bayesian methods provide an approximate approach to this task, but inferring the sequence of hidden states is a particularly challenging implementation step. The authors focus on making that step easier to express and carry out.

Their method converts the hidden-state inference problem into a form handled by standard Kalman filtering and smoothing recursions. This connects variational Bayesian inference to established state-space computations, providing a unified formulation where earlier published approaches used belief propagation. The contribution is a reformulation that makes existing inference machinery directly usable.

The authors demonstrate the approach through Bayesian temporal independent component analysis, applied to finding independent dynamical processes beneath noisy EEG measurements. This example connects the general framework to recovering hidden temporal structure from observations. The broader significance is implementation simplicity: placing the difficult hidden-state calculation within familiar filtering and smoothing procedures can make future variational Bayesian applications easier to develop.
neurips-2006-unified-inference-for-varia.tldr: A reformulation lets variational Bayesian state-space models use standard Kalman filtering and smoothing for hidden-state inference.
